The Work, Torah Teaching and Exegetical Method of Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon HaLevi Bokrat
His Life and Historical-Cultural Background
Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon HaLevi Bokrat (also known as al-Bokrat, Abokrat or Bukrat) was one of the most prominent sages of Spain in the generation of the expulsion and one of the important commentators on Scripture and halakha in North Africa at the threshold of the modern era [cite: 1]. Bokrat grew up and was educated in the city of Málaga in the region of Andalusia, in southern Spain, a cultural and spiritual center in which Talmudic study, Hebrew linguistics and the general sciences flourished together [cite: 1]. In this diverse environment Bokrat acquired comprehensive knowledge of the Arabic and Spanish languages, alongside expertise in the natural sciences, astronomy and grammar, which later served him as the foundation of his exegetical and Torah work [cite: 1].
The decree of the expulsion from Spain in the year 5252 (1492) cut off Jewish creativity in the Iberian Peninsula and was one of the formative events of his life [cite: 1]. Like many members of his community, Rabbi Abraham Bokrat was forced to leave his home in Málaga, and a short time later he found refuge in the city of Tunis in North Africa [cite: 1]. In Tunis, which became one of the important centers of absorption for the sages of Andalusia, a rich and prolonged creative chapter of his life began [cite: 1]. There he established his standing as a spiritual leader, a liturgical poet and a respondent to halakhic queries, and there he completed his central Torah works [cite: 1].
In historical and rabbinic scholarship it is very important to distinguish between Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon HaLevi Bokrat and his contemporary, Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon of Torrutiel [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5]. Whereas Torrutiel was born in 1482, wandered after the expulsion to the city of Fez in Morocco and became famous as a historiographer who composed the supplement to the "Sefer ha-Kabbalah" of the Raavad [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5], Bokrat established the center of his activity in Tunis, and his focus was on biblical exegesis, grammar, poetry and halakhic ruling [cite: 1].
"Sefer ha-Zikkaron": The Exegetical Enterprise on Rashi's Commentary on the Torah
The most prominent Torah achievement of Rabbi Abraham Bokrat's life is "Sefer ha-Zikkaron" (The Book of Remembrance), which he wrote and completed in the city of Tunis in the year 5267 (1507) [cite: 1]. The work belongs to the genre of supercommentaries on Rashi's commentary on the Torah and is regarded by scholars and commentators as one of the most profound, precise and excellent works ever written on Rashi's commentary [cite: 1, 6].
The writing of "Sefer ha-Zikkaron" in the first decade of the 16th century arose from the burning need of the generation of the exiles to preserve and consolidate the enduring treasures of biblical exegesis. Rashi's commentary on the Torah served as the basis of daily study in all the communities of Israel, but over the years and through the copying of manuscripts corruptions crept into it, and the precise exegetical motives behind it were lost from view. Bokrat set himself the goal of establishing the original text of Rashi's commentary, of examining the grammatical and syntactic precision of his words, and of resolving the difficulties raised against him by the later medieval commentators.
Bokrat's exegetical methodology in "Sefer ha-Zikkaron" is marked by sharp textual analysis. He consistently investigates the "diyuka" in the verse, that is, what linguistic, substantive or theological difficulty in the biblical text led Rashi to depart from the plain meaning of the text and to incorporate a particular midrash of the Sages [cite: 7, 8]. At the same time, Bokrat deals directly with the objections of the later sages of Spain, foremost among them Nahmanides (Ramban), Rabbenu Abraham ibn Ezra and the Radak. Whereas Nahmanides frequently challenges Rashi's plain interpretations and midrashic readings, Bokrat comes to Rashi's defense and shows how his position rests on the foundations of the Sages and on a deep syntactic understanding.
The importance of "Sefer ha-Zikkaron" did not escape the sages of the following generations, but the work remained in manuscript for about 340 years. It was first printed in the city of Livorno in Italy in the year 5605 (1845) by Shadal (Samuel David Luzzatto), who recognized its scholarly and Torah value, proofread it and appended a detailed introduction to it [cite: 1].
The Enterprise of Translation, Poetry and Halakha
Alongside his exegetical work on Scripture, Rabbi Abraham Bokrat was active in further Torah and cultural arenas, which reflected his spiritual versatility. According to historical and bibliographical research, Bokrat translated the halakhic responsa of Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi (the Rif) from Judeo-Arabic into the Holy Tongue [cite: 1]. This translation enterprise was of the first importance, since it enabled decisors and students in Europe and in communities that did not command Arabic to gain direct access to the responsa of the Rif and to incorporate them into the literature of halakhic ruling.
Bokrat also stood out as a liturgical poet and a religious poet [cite: 1]. His poetry combined the meter and aesthetics of classical Andalusian poetry with themes of faith, repentance, lament over the hardships of the expulsion and longing for redemption [cite: 1]. His poetic work served not only as an emotional expression of the national catastrophe of the uprooting of Spanish Jewry, but also as a tool for teaching the foundations of theology and ethics.
Bokrat's family and spiritual legacy continued to resonate in the Middle East in the following generations. The sources indicate that his grandson (or a family member of the next generation), Rabbi Abraham ben Isaac HaLevi Abokrat, was active in Egypt in the 16th century and was one of the prominent sages of the community, a man of wide learning, of great wealth and the owner of a library rich in rare manuscripts [cite: 1].
His Torah Teaching and Hermeneutic Conception: An In-Depth Analysis
A comprehensive look at the work of Rabbi Abraham Bokrat yields deep insights into his Torah teaching and his place in the history of Jewish thought. His teaching represents the late medieval Andalusian outlook, which sees the Torah and the general sciences as a single unified system. Bokrat felt no contradiction between his mastery of the natural sciences and foreign languages and his immersion in the interpretation of halakha and Scripture; rather, he harnessed scientific and philological tools in the service of Torah exposition [cite: 1].
The genre of supercommentary that he developed in "Sefer ha-Zikkaron" functioned as a mechanism of cultural and identity rehabilitation. Following the destruction of the Torah centers in Spain and the geographical dispersion of the exiles, turning Rashi's commentary into a canonical text that calls for explanation, defense and meticulous analysis served as a bridge between the tradition of Ashkenaz and France (from which Rashi had grown) and the Andalusian tradition. Bokrat applied the rules of grammar and logic of the sages of Spain to justify Rashi's decisions, and thereby contributed to the creation of an inter-communal exegetical synthesis.
In addition, the shift of the center of gravity of his work to the Maghreb lay at the basis of the growth of new Torah centers in Tunisia and North Africa. The presence of brilliant sages such as Bokrat in Tunis enriched the local world of learning with Andalusian analytical patterns, and ensured the continuity of the exegetical and halakhic chain even under conditions of exile and political upheaval.
Comparative Table and Structured Summary: The Focal Points of Rabbi Abraham Bokrat's Work
Focus of activity | Description and main characteristics | Historical and Torah contribution | Sources
Biblical exegesis | The composition of "Sefer ha-Zikkaron" (Tunis, 1507), a comprehensive supercommentary on Rashi on the Torah. | Resolving the objections of Nahmanides and Ibn Ezra, correcting textual versions, and clarifying Rashi's exegetical motive. | [cite: 1, 6]
Halakhic translation | Translation of the responsa of the Rif from Judeo-Arabic into the Holy Tongue. | Making the halakhic rulings of the Rif accessible to students in Europe and in communities that do not speak Arabic. | [cite: 1]
Poetry and piyyut | Writing piyyutim and poems in the Andalusian meter. | Theological, intellectual and emotional expression of the hardships of the expulsion and of the longing for redemption. | [cite: 1]
Scientific education | Mastery of the natural sciences, astronomy, the Arabic language and Spanish. | Incorporating scientific and philological tools into Torah analysis and exegesis. | [cite: 1]
Historical distinction | Distinguished from Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon of Torrutiel (a man of Fez, author of the supplement to "Sefer ha-Kabbalah"). | Preventing bibliographical confusion between sages of the generation of the expulsion who went to North Africa. | [cite: 1, 2, 3, 5]
Conclusions
Rabbi Abraham ben Solomon HaLevi Bokrat embodies the figure of the Spanish sage who combines in the paths of his creativity the worlds of Torah, science, language and poetry [cite: 1]. His central work, "Sefer ha-Zikkaron," remains to this day an enduring treasure of the exegetical literature on Rashi's commentary, and it attests to scholarly power, philological precision and a brilliant analytical ability [cite: 1, 6].
His multidisciplinary contribution (from the translation of the responsa of the Rif, through the writing of piyyutim and the defense of the exegetical tradition, to the transfer of the spiritual wealth of Andalusia to the communities of Tunisia and North Africa) places him in the front rank of the sages of Israel in the generation of the transition from the Middle Ages to the modern era [cite: 1].
